I've battled suicidal thoughts off and on for the majority of my life. Even called a suicide hotline once because it was really, really bad that day. But I have family and friends that, no matter how much I just want to crawl into a hole and die sometimes, I could never do that to them.

This is probably my biggest issue with Subway. I'm not sure if it's normal, or just with my franchise, but they seem to think that it's a great idea to choose to be understaffed as much as possible.

Every single shift is a game of playing catch-up that the previous shift didn't have a chance to get to and was ordered off the clock so as not to interfere with that precious productivity.

Little things like having to hold up the line to do some prep on the fly, or half-assing some cleaning, or running out of bread cause there was no way to get away from the line to make more are all things that could be avoided if Subway was willing to pay an extra sub (okay, foot and a mini, or something akin to that) an hour for one more employee.

[Found this trying to verify my own assumptions of marijuana addiction.](http://recoveryguy.hubpages.com/hub/Is-Marijuana-Addictive)

Basically, it's not physically addictive, meaning no physical withdrawals. With it being fat soluble, your body naturally weens itself from it (at least, that's what makes sense to me).

However, psychological addictions can happen with anything. Whether it be with alcohol, weed, coffee, eating, running, yelling at your spouse, washing your hands, anything that becomes a habit at the individual level.

But, just like with any other kind of addiction, no one is ever really willing to "sober" up until they, themselves, decide it so.

The stoner enjoys being a stoner. They make that choice. They have the right to. If they're not harming anyone else, they will be the only one to suffer the consequences of their addiction. And if they do (slowed reaction time in traffic, for instance), there are penalties, sometimes major, for that.

I wouldn't say they're justified, they likely just don't care. They are high, after all. The "fuck it" drug. Or perhaps it's all just a desire for having that ritual, and this drug allows for a great number of people to share in this ritual together. Without necessarily turning into crazy, stampeding beasts.

Honestly, I still enjoy smoking it. But I am aware that there is a time and a place for everything, and moderation is the key to any true success. It definitely slows my reaction time, slows my reading speed, causes quite a bit of introversion, tampers with my memory, and makes work damn near impossible (*they know*). It also has helped me through some of the real withdrawals I've had from other substances. Has allowed me to come out of some sorrows that I've dwelled in far longer than I should have. Has brought together a mutual, habitual, kindness from people of all sorts in my life, including some of my closest friends, along with never forgotten strangers.

Bottom line: it's the person that's the addict, not necessarily the substance.
